content.heading: 4.4 Coordinate Systems
content.paragraph: An important reason for specifying a basis $B$ for a vector space $V$ is to impose a “coordinate system” on $V$. This section will show that if $B$ contains $n$ vectors, then the coordinate system will make $V$ act like ${\mathbb{R}}^{n}$. If $V$ is already ${\mathbb{R}}^{n}$ itself, then $B$ will determine a coordinate system that gives a new “view” of $V$.
The existence of coordinate systems rests on the following fundamental result.

content.heading: A Graphical Interpretation of Coordinates
content.paragraph: A coordinate system on a set consists of a one-to-one mapping of the points in the set into ${\mathbb{R}}^{n}$. For example, ordinary graph paper provides a coordinate system for the plane when one selects perpendicular axes and a unit of measurement on each axis. Figure 1 shows the standard basis $\left\{ \mathbf{e}_{1}\text{,~}\mathbf{e}_{2} \right\}$, the vectors $\mathbf{b}_{1}( = \mathbf{e}_{1})$ and $\mathbf{b}_{2}$ from Example 1, and the vector $\mathbf{x} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 6 \end{bmatrix}$. The coordinates $1$ and $6$ give the location of $\mathbf{x}$ relative to the standard basis: $1$ unit in the $\mathbf{e}_{1}$ direction and $6$ units in the $\mathbf{e}_{2}$ direction.

example.paragraph: In crystallography, the description of a crystal lattice is aided by choosing a basis $\{\mathbf{u}\text{,~}\mathbf{v}\text{,~}\mathbf{w}\}$ for ${\mathbb{R}}^{3}$ that corresponds to three adjacent edges of one “unit cell” of the crystal. An analogous change of coordinates can be carried out in ${\mathbb{R}}^{n}$ for a basis $B = \left\{ \mathbf{b}_{1}\text{,}\ldots,~\mathbf{b}_{n} \right\}$. Let

(4)$$\boxed{\mathbf{x} = P_{B}\left\lbrack \mathbf{x} \right\rbrack_{B}}$$

We call $P_{B}$ the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to the standard basis in $\text{ℝ}^{n}$. Left-multiplication by $P_{B}$ transforms the coordinate vector $\left\lbrack \mathbf{x} \right\rbrack_{B}$ into $\mathbf{x}$. The change-of-coordinates equation (4) is important and will be needed at several points in Chapters 5 and 7.

Since the columns of $P_{B}$ form a basis for ${\mathbb{R}}^{n}$, $P_{B}$ is invertible (by the Invertible Matrix Theorem). Left-multiplication by $P_{B}^{- 1}$ converts $\mathbf{x}$ into its $B\text{-coordinate}$ vector:

The correspondence $\mathbf{x}\mapsto\!\left\lbrack \mathbf{x} \right\rbrack_{B}$, produced here by $P_{B}^{- 1}$, is the coordinate mapping mentioned earlier. Since $P_{B}^{- 1}$ is an invertible matrix, the coordinate mapping is a one-to-one linear transformation from ${\mathbb{R}}^{n}$ onto $\text{ℝ}^{n}$, by the Invertible Matrix Theorem. (See also Theorem 12 in Section 1.9.) This property of the coordinate mapping is also true in a general vector space that has a basis, as we shall see.
content.heading: The Coordinate Mapping
content.paragraph: Choosing a basis $B = \left\{ \mathbf{b}_{1}\text{,}\text{…}\text{,~}\mathbf{b}_{n} \right\}$ for a vector space $V$ introduces a coordinate system in $V$. The coordinate mapping $\mathbf{x}\mapsto\mathbf{\left\lbrack { x} \right\rbrack}_{B}$ connects the possibly unfamiliar space $V$ to the familiar space ${\mathbb{R}}^{n}$. See Figure 5. Points in $V$ can now be identified by their new “names.”

figure.caption: The coordinate mapping from V onto ℝn﻿

Thus the coordinate mapping also preserves scalar multiplication and hence is a linear transformation. See Exercises 27 and 28 for verification that the coordinate mapping is one-to-one and maps $V$ onto ${\mathbb{R}}^{n}$.

The linearity of the coordinate mapping extends to linear combinations, just as in Section 1.8. If $\mathbf{u}_{1}\text{,}\text{…}\text{,~}\mathbf{u}_{p}$ are in $V$ and if $c_{1}\text{,}\text{…}\text{,~}c_{p}$ are scalars, then
In words, (5) says that the $B\text{-coordinate}$ vector of a linear combination of $\mathbf{u}_{1}\text{,}\text{…}\text{,~}\mathbf{u}_{p}$ is the same linear combination of their coordinate vectors.

The coordinate mapping in Theorem 9 is an important example of an isomorphism from $V$ onto ${\mathbb{R}}^{n}$. In general, a one-to-one linear transformation from a vector space $V$ onto a vector space $W$ is called an isomorphism from $V$ onto $W$ (iso from the Greek for “the same,” and morph from the Greek for “form” or “structure”). The notation and terminology for $V$ and $W$ may differ, but the two spaces are indistinguishable as vector spaces. Every vector space calculation in$V$is accurately reproduced in$W$, and vice versa. In particular, any real vector space with a basis of $n$ vectors is indistinguishable from $\text{ℝ}^{n}$. See Exercises 29 and 30.

Since $\mathbf{p}$ is already displayed as a linear combination of the standard basis vectors, we conclude that

Thus the coordinate mapping $\mathbf{p}\mapsto\left\lbrack {\mathbf{p}} \right\rbrack_{B}$ is an isomorphism from ${\mathbb{P}}_{3}$ onto $\text{ℝ}^{4}$. All vector space operations in ${\mathbb{P}}_{3}$ correspond to operations in $\text{ℝ}^{4}$.

content.paragraph: If we think of ${\mathbb{P}}_{3}$ and $\text{ℝ}^{4}$ as displays on two computer screens that are connected via the coordinate mapping, then every vector space operation in ${\mathbb{P}}_{3}$ on one screen is exactly duplicated by a corresponding vector operation in $\text{ℝ}^{4}$ on the other screen. The vectors on the ${\mathbb{P}}_{3}$ screen look different from those on the $\text{ℝ}^{4}$ screen, but they “act” as vectors in exactly the same way. See Figure 6.
